course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 9

unit.title: Decimals, Percentages and Rounding
unit.blurb: Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10, calculating with decimals, compound percentages, and upper and lower bounds.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Multiply and divide numbers by 10 to any positive or negative power, e.g. 10³, 10⁻², and by 0.1 and 0.01.

O2.t: Multiply and divide by decimals, using estimation to check answers.

O3.t: Understand compound percentages, e.g. a 10% increase followed by a 10% decrease, and calculate repeated percentage change.

O4.t: Find the upper and lower bounds of a number rounded to a given degree of accuracy.

sections.title: Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10

p: A computer chip has transistors **5 × 10⁻⁹ m** wide. An engineer needs to know how many fit across a **0.003 m** strip.
What does multiplying or dividing by 10⁻⁹ actually do to a number? Think about it before you read on.
**× 10ⁿ** (n positive): digits move n places to the left (the number gets bigger). **÷ 10ⁿ**: digits move n places right.
**× 10⁻ⁿ** is the same as **÷ 10ⁿ**, and **÷ 10⁻ⁿ** is the same as **× 10ⁿ**.
10⁻² = 1/100, so multiplying by 10⁻² means multiplying by 1/100, which is dividing by 100.
Dividing by 10⁻³ means dividing by 1/1000, which is the same as multiplying by 1000.

lesson.t: How do I multiply or divide by a power of 10?
p: Step 1: Rewrite: × 10⁻ⁿ → ÷ 10ⁿ; ÷ 10⁻ⁿ → × 10ⁿ.
Step 2: Count the zeros (n).
Step 3: Move the digits n places (left to make bigger, right to make smaller).
Step 4: Check the size: should it be bigger or smaller?

captions: A computer chip has parts that are 5 times 10 to the power negative 9 metres wide.
An engineer works with numbers like this every day.
Does multiplying by 10 to the power negative 9 make a positive number smaller, or bigger?
Pause the video and choose.
10 to the power negative 9 is 1 over 1,000,000,000.
Multiplying by it is the same as dividing by a billion.
So the number gets much smaller.
Remember: 10 cubed is 1,000.
10 to the power 0 is 1.
And 10 to the power negative 2 is 0.01.
Multiplying by 10 to a positive power moves the digits to the left, so the number gets bigger.
Dividing moves them to the right.
Multiplying by 10 to a negative power is the same as dividing.
And dividing by 10 to a negative power is the same as multiplying.
Your turn.
Work out 4.7 times 10 to the power negative 2.
Pause the video and try it.
Times 10 to the negative 2 means divide by 100.
Move the digits 2 places to the right: 0.047.
Why does it work?
10 to the negative 2 is 1 hundredth.
Multiplying by 1 hundredth is dividing by 100.
Here is the method.
Step 1: rewrite it.
Times 10 to the negative N means divide by 10 to the N.
Divide by 10 to the negative N means multiply by 10 to the N.
Step 2: N tells you how many places.
Step 3: move the digits.
Left to make it bigger, right to make it smaller.
Step 4: check the size.
Should the answer be bigger or smaller?
Work out 0.072 divided by 10 to the negative 2.
Dividing by 10 to the negative 2 is the same as multiplying by 100.
So the answer is 7.2.
Your turn.

Pause and work it out.
Dividing by 10 to the negative 3 means multiplying by 1,000.
250 times 10 to the N is 0.025.
Find N.
To get from 250 to 0.025, the digits move 4 places to the right.
That is dividing by 10,000, so N is negative 4.
How many 5 nanometre parts fit across a 0.003 metre strip?
0.003 divided by 5 times 10 to the negative 9 is 0.0006 times 10 to the 9, which is 600,000.
Leo works out 5.4 times 10 to the negative 1.
Which line is wrong?
Line 1 is wrong.
Times 10 to the negative 1 means divide by 10.
It makes the number smaller.
5.4 divided by 10 is 0.54.
Scientists switch between metres, micrometres and nanometres using powers of 10.
A nanometre is 10 to the negative 9 metres.
A human hair is about 80,000 nanometres wide.
One last question.
Work out 82 times 10 to the negative 1.
Pause the video and answer.

82 divided by 10 is 8.2.
To remember: times 10 to the negative N is the same as divide by 10 to the N.
Divide by 10 to the negative N is the same as multiply by 10 to the N.

p: A driver fills **0.4 of a 52-litre tank** with petrol. Later, a **$38.48** fuel bill is shared between friends who each pay **$4.81**.
Without a calculator, how could you work out 0.4 × 52, or how many friends shared the bill? Think about it before you read on.
Multiply the whole numbers, then adjust for the decimal places: the answer has as many decimal places as the two numbers together.
Make the divisor a whole number by multiplying **both** numbers by the same power of 10 – the answer doesn't change.
Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive number **bigger**.

p: Step 1: Estimate the answer.

Step 3: ÷: multiply both numbers by 10, 100… until the divisor is whole, then divide.
Step 4: Compare with your estimate.

p: Ravi puts **$2000** in a savings account that pays **4% interest each year**, added to the account. Interest is then paid on the interest too.
How much after 3 years? Is it just 3 × 4% = 12% more? Try it before you read on.
Increase by 20% → × 1.2; decrease by 20% → × 0.8.
A **compound percentage** change applies a percentage again and again, each time to the **new** amount.
Use the multiplier once for each year: 2000 × 1.04 × 1.04 × 1.04 = 2000 × 1.04³.
p2: After 3 years: **$2249.73** – more than $2240 (12% simple interest).

p: Values that fall each year (a car loses 15% a year) use a multiplier less than 1: value = start × 0.85ⁿ.
Different changes multiply together: +10% then −10% gives × 1.1 × 0.9 = × 0.99 – a 1% **decrease** overall, not 0%.

Step 4: Round only at the end (money: 2 d.p.).

p: A news report says **'65 000 fans'** watched a match, rounded to the nearest thousand.
What is the smallest and largest the real crowd could have been? Think about it before you read on.
4.36 to 1 d.p. is 4.4; 2450 to the nearest 100 is 2500.
A rounded value stands for a range. The **lower bound** is the smallest value that rounds to it; the **upper bound** is the boundary above, which rounds **up** to the next value.
Go **half a unit** down and up: 65 000 to the nearest 1000 → 64 500 ≤ n < 65 500.
Write the range as an inequality: **4.65 ≤ L < 4.75**. The lower bound is included (≤); the upper bound is not (<) because 4.75 rounds up to 4.8.
For counting (discrete) data like the crowd, the largest possible value is 65 499.

qq.prompt: A length is 8.3 cm to 1 d.p. Lower bound (cm)?

lesson.t: How do I find upper and lower bounds?
p: Step 1: Identify the accuracy (the unit it was rounded to).
Step 2: Halve that unit.
Step 3: Lower bound = value − half; upper bound = value + half.
Step 4: Write lower ≤ x < upper.

Engineers give tolerances (10 mm ± 0.05 mm) so parts fit; headline numbers are usually rounded.
Bounds are half a unit either side.
lower ≤ x < upper.
